songs:counting-the-miles.text: Counting the miles from the passenger seat
Every sign a promise I don't read
The horizon leans and the radio hums
A pocket full of nowhere to go
I count the miles that the road has kept
Every one of them a promise I forgot
The coffee's cold and the window's white
And somewhere north a town I used to know
I count the miles in the passenger seat
And leave the ones I never will regret
Every mile is a door I haven't opened
Every mile is a song I haven't written

songs:paper-boats.text: Fold the paper, fold it twice
Put a hat on top and watch it fly
Down the steps and down the rain
Take the page and fold it well
Send it off where waters swell
Fold the paper, fold it twice
Every child is worth a chance
Down the steps and down the rain

songs:morning-market.text: Six in the morning and the crates arrive
Someone is stacking them against the wall
First of the season and the best of it all
Two for a pound and I'll take the whole crate
Hey, you want these or you want those?
Money changes hands and the morning grows
Everything here has a story to sell
You can ask the seller how it used to be
Six in the morning and the light is thin
By eight o'clock the whole street is in
Buy it while it's cheap, come back at noon
The best of the market is gone by then

songs:the-long-way-round.text: I had taken the road that everyone praised
And I had reasons, and I had been certain
But the long way round is the way that stays
Because it taught me what the river knows
If you had asked me, I would have said no
If you had asked me, I would have gone
But nobody asked, and here I am
With dust on my shoes and dust on my hands
The long way round is the way that stays
And what the river knows, I know as well
I had taken the road that everyone praised
And it led me here, and it led me well

podcasts:the-practice-room-ep1.speaker: Nina
podcasts:the-practice-room-ep1.text: Welcome to The Practice Room. I'm Nina. Today we are going to do something that looks lazy and is not: we are going to sing along with a song in English, badly, and that is the point.

podcasts:the-practice-room-ep1.speaker: Nina
podcasts:the-practice-room-ep1.text: Most learners try to understand a song first. They listen, they look up every word, they try to translate the whole thing, and by the time they have understood it, they have lost the thread. Understanding a song is not the first step. Singing it is.

podcasts:the-practice-room-ep1.speaker: Nina
podcasts:the-practice-room-ep1.text: Here is the method. Five steps, fifteen minutes. First, listen once without the text. Just hear the shape of it. Notice where the music goes up and where it comes down.

podcasts:the-practice-room-ep1.speaker: Nina
podcasts:the-practice-room-ep1.text: Second, read the lyrics with your finger under the line. Not out loud yet. Your eye needs to find the lines first, because your mouth is going to have to find them later.

podcasts:the-practice-room-ep1.speaker: Nina
podcasts:the-practice-room-ep1.text: Third, sing. Badly. Nobody is listening. You are not singing for accuracy, you are singing for timing. You are training your mouth to arrive at the same moment as the singer.

podcasts:the-practice-room-ep1.speaker: Nina
podcasts:the-practice-room-ep1.text: Fourth, shadow. Now you follow the voice in real time, half a word behind, like a shadow. This is the hard part and it is the useful part. It trains your ear and your mouth at the same time.

podcasts:the-practice-room-ep1.speaker: Nina
podcasts:the-practice-room-ep1.text: And fifth, one line only. Pick the single line you liked best and sing it ten times until it is yours. Not the song. The line.

podcasts:the-practice-room-ep1.speaker: Nina
podcasts:the-practice-room-ep1.text: That is the whole method. Notice what is not in it: no dictionary, no grammar, no app that tells you your pronunciation was wrong. You need about fifteen minutes and a song you already like.

podcasts:the-practice-room-ep1.speaker: Nina
podcasts:the-practice-room-ep1.text: Try it now with Counting the Miles. Start with the first step: one listen, no text. Then come back and tell me how it went.

podcasts:el-sonido-del-cafe-ep1.speaker: Lucía
podcasts:el-sonido-del-cafe-ep1.text: Hello, and welcome to El Sonido del Café. I'm Lucía, and today we are going to taste a place without tasting it. We are going to talk about how a coffee bean can taste of the hill it grew on.

podcasts:el-sonido-del-cafe-ep1.speaker: Lucía
podcasts:el-sonido-del-cafe-ep1.text: Picture a farm in the coffee-growing region of Colombia. The farm is not flat. It is a set of steep green slopes, and at the top of each slope the temperature is a little cooler than at the bottom.

podcasts:el-sonido-del-cafe-ep1.speaker: Lucía
podcasts:el-sonido-del-cafe-ep1.text: That difference of a few degrees is enough to change the bean. The cold nights slow the ripening, so the seed inside stays small and sweet, and the fruit around it turns a deep red. Those red fruits are called cherries, even though they are not fruit at all.

podcasts:el-sonido-del-cafe-ep1.speaker: Lucía
podcasts:el-sonido-del-cafe-ep1.text: Now the harvest. In Colombia most coffee is picked by hand, and this is not nostalgia. A machine can strip a branch in two seconds, but it takes the ripe cherries and the green ones together.

podcasts:el-sonido-del-cafe-ep1.speaker: Lucía
podcasts:el-sonido-del-cafe-ep1.text: So pickers walk the rows, and they look. They look for the colour, they feel the weight, and they take only what is right. A good picker can pick about sixty kilos of cherries in a day, and they can tell you the name of every farm on the slope.

podcasts:el-sonido-del-cafe-ep1.speaker: Lucía
podcasts:el-sonido-del-cafe-ep1.text: That name matters. Single-origin coffee is not a marketing word invented last year. It is an old promise: this cup came from this farm, this family, this hillside, in this year.

podcasts:el-sonido-del-cafe-ep1.speaker: Lucía
podcasts:el-sonido-del-cafe-ep1.text: And the last thing is the drying. The beans leave the farm as mucilage, a sticky layer like honey, and they are dried on patios or in parabolic beds under the sun for up to two weeks.

podcasts:el-sonido-del-cafe-ep1.speaker: Lucía
podcasts:el-sonido-del-cafe-ep1.text: During that time, whoever turns the beans is making decisions. Too much sun and they bake. Too little and they mould. A good worker reads the humidity in the afternoon and decides how thick to spread the layer.

podcasts:el-sonido-del-cafe-ep1.speaker: Lucía
podcasts:el-sonido-del-cafe-ep1.text: So when you drink a coffee that tastes of chocolate, or of orange, or of nothing in particular, none of that happened in your kitchen. It happened on a slope, in a season, in the hands of somebody you will never meet.

podcasts:focus-and-noise-ep1.speaker: Nina
podcasts:focus-and-noise-ep1.text: This is episode two of The Practice Room, and today we are talking about noise, which is either the best thing that has ever happened to your focus or the worst.

podcasts:focus-and-noise-ep1.speaker: Nina
podcasts:focus-and-noise-ep1.text: There is a well-known experiment from the nineties about this. Two groups of people did the same task. One group worked in silence and one worked with noise. The noisy group performed better on dull tasks and much worse on tasks that needed thought.

podcasts:focus-and-noise-ep1.speaker: Nina
podcasts:focus-and-noise-ep1.text: That is the whole story, really. Noise is not good or bad for your brain. It is good for one kind of work and terrible for another, and the mistake is using the wrong tool for the job.

podcasts:focus-and-noise-ep1.speaker: Nina
podcasts:focus-and-noise-ep1.text: So if you are doing something repetitive, something mechanical, something where your hands are busy and the decision-making is small, then background noise can carry you a long way. The music becomes a rhythm for the hands.

podcasts:focus-and-noise-ep1.speaker: Nina
podcasts:focus-and-noise-ep1.text: But if you are writing an argument, learning a language, or reading something you do not fully understand, then noise eats the part of your attention that holds the sentence in place. You read the line three times and still lose it at the end.

podcasts:focus-and-noise-ep1.speaker: Nina
podcasts:focus-and-noise-ep1.text: Here is what works if you cannot change your room. First, separate the noise from the task with headphones. Even headphones with no music playing will cut the sharp edges, and you can use the music at a volume low enough to disappear.

podcasts:focus-and-noise-ep1.speaker: Nina
podcasts:focus-and-noise-ep1.text: Second, give the hard task a fixed place and a fixed time. People protect what has a slot in the calendar much better than what is supposed to happen whenever there is a gap.

podcasts:focus-and-noise-ep1.speaker: Nina
podcasts:focus-and-noise-ep1.text: And third, keep one sound for one kind of work. If the same music plays while you write and while you rest, you stop learning what it means. Give the studying its own sound and the resting its own silence.

podcasts:cosas-del-metro-ep1.speaker: Andrés
podcasts:cosas-del-metro-ep1.text: Welcome to Cosas del Metro. I am Andrés, and this week: the words you only learn when you travel. Every day, for a year, on the same line.

podcasts:cosas-del-metro-ep1.speaker: Andrés
podcasts:cosas-del-metro-ep1.text: Nobody teaches you the vocabulary of a station. You learn it because you need it. The announcement says the name of the next station and you want to know whether you have to get up now or two stops later.

podcasts:cosas-del-metro-ep1.speaker: Andrés
podcasts:cosas-del-metro-ep1.text: So you learn 'the next stop'. You learn 'the last stop', because the driver says it at the end of the line and you finally know where you are. You learn 'connection', which in English is 'transfer'.

podcasts:cosas-del-metro-ep1.speaker: Andrés
podcasts:cosas-del-metro-ep1.text: And you learn the small politeness of a shared space. 'Excuse me.' 'Sorry, is this seat taken?' You learn them standing up, with your bag on your shoulder, and they stick in a way that a classroom sentence never does.

podcasts:cosas-del-metro-ep1.speaker: Andrés
podcasts:cosas-del-metro-ep1.text: Then there is the vocabulary of delay. When the line stops for four minutes with no announcement, people look around. And then somebody says, in a voice that is not really a question: 'Is it running?'

podcasts:cosas-del-metro-ep1.speaker: Andrés
podcasts:cosas-del-metro-ep1.text: Four words, one grammatical mistake, and a completely different meaning. 'Is it running' means 'is it moving again'. 'Is it running' does not mean 'is the service operating'. In English, a small wrong word can change the whole question.

podcasts:cosas-del-metro-ep1.speaker: Andrés
podcasts:cosas-del-metro-ep1.text: I do not think teachers should stop using textbooks. But I do think a language is also the set of words a city hands you for free, every morning, whether you are ready or not.

podcasts:cosas-del-metro-ep1.speaker: Andrés
podcasts:cosas-del-metro-ep1.text: So the exercise for this week is simple. On your next trip, write down ten words you did not know on Monday. Ten is enough. Then use five of them badly tonight, in a sentence about your day.

films:the-last-tram.speaker: Narrator
films:the-last-tram.line: The last tram leaves the square at eleven forty.
films:the-last-tram.translation: El último tranvía sale de la plaza a las once y cuarenta.

films:the-last-tram.speaker: Narrator
films:the-last-tram.line: By then the shops have closed and the square belongs to the people who have nowhere else to be.
films:the-last-tram.translation: Para entonces las tiendas han cerrado y la plaza es de quienes no tienen otro sitio donde estar.

films:the-last-tram.speaker: Old man
films:the-last-tram.line: Then I will wait for you.

films:the-last-tram.speaker: Narrator
films:the-last-tram.line: He says it as if it were obvious. As if waiting for a tram at midnight were a thing that people did every night of their lives.
films:the-last-tram.translation: Lo dice como si fuera obvio. Como si esperar un tranvía a medianoche fuera algo que la gente hiciera todas las noches de su vida.

films:the-last-tram.speaker: Driver
films:the-last-tram.line: You will be here when I come back.
films:the-last-tram.translation: Usted estará aquí cuando yo vuelva.

films:the-last-tram.speaker: Old man
films:the-last-tram.line: I will be here when you come back.

films:the-last-tram.speaker: Narrator
films:the-last-tram.line: The doors close. The tram takes the square, and the two of them watch each other through the glass.
films:the-last-tram.translation: Las puertas se cierran. El tranvía cruza la plaza y los dos se miran a través del vidrio.

films:the-last-tram.speaker: Narrator
films:the-last-tram.line: The square is empty again. But something in it has changed, and nobody will say what.
films:the-last-tram.translation: La plaza vuelve a estar vacía. Pero algo en ella ha cambiado, y nadie dirá qué.

films:paper-and-ink.speaker: Narrator
films:paper-and-ink.line: He has been coming to the workshop for eleven years. He brings the same book every time.
films:paper-and-ink.translation: Lleva once años viniendo al taller. Trae siempre el mismo libro.

films:paper-and-ink.speaker: Narrator
films:paper-and-ink.line: The book is called A Handbook of Correspondence. It was printed in nineteen fifty-four, and it is still, according to the owner, the only book about the subject that has ever been written.
films:paper-and-ink.translation: El libro se titula Manual de correspondencia. Se imprimió en mil novecientos cincuenta y cuatro y sigue siendo, según el dueño, el único libro sobre el tema que se ha escrito.

films:paper-and-ink.speaker: Binder
films:paper-and-ink.line: Ninety-one pages. Fifty-one of them are about envelopes.
films:paper-and-ink.translation: Noventa y una páginas. Cincuenta y una son sobre sobres.

films:paper-and-ink.speaker: Man
films:paper-and-ink.line: Envelopes are the difficult part. Paper is easy.
films:paper-and-ink.translation: Los sobres son la parte difícil. El papel es fácil.

films:paper-and-ink.speaker: Binder
films:paper-and-ink.line: You are not writing a letter. You are choosing a letter.
films:paper-and-ink.translation: Usted no está escribiendo una carta. Está eligiendo una carta.

films:paper-and-ink.speaker: Narrator
films:paper-and-ink.line: He says this without any weight. Then he looks at the book for a while, and corrects himself.
films:paper-and-ink.translation: Lo dice sin ninguna ironía. Luego mira el libro un rato y se corrige.

films:paper-and-ink.speaker: Man
films:paper-and-ink.line: You are not choosing a letter. You are choosing not to send one.
films:paper-and-ink.translation: Usted no está eligiendo una carta. Está eligiendo no enviar ninguna.

films:paper-and-ink.speaker: Narrator
films:paper-and-ink.line: The binder does not answer. She ties the pages, trims the edges, and sets the book on the shelf with the others, where it will wait.
films:paper-and-ink.translation: La encuadernadora no contesta. Ata las páginas, recorta los bordes y pone el libro en la estantería con los demás, donde esperará.

films:paper-and-ink.speaker: Narrator
films:paper-and-ink.line: He will be back on Thursday. He will bring the same book.
films:paper-and-ink.translation: Volverá el jueves. Traerá el mismo libro.

films:night-shift-observatory.speaker: Narrator
films:night-shift-observatory.line: The dome opens at sunset and closes at sunrise, and between those two events the observatory belongs to whoever is on shift.
films:night-shift-observatory.translation: La cúpula se abre al atardecer y se cierra al amanecer, y entre esos dos hechos el observatorio pertenece a quien esté de turno.

films:night-shift-observatory.speaker: Dr. Reyes
films:night-shift-observatory.line: Meridian transit in forty minutes. Coffee number two is wrong, by the way. Somebody left the sugar out.
films:night-shift-observatory.translation: Tránsito meridiano en cuarenta minutos. Por cierto, el café número dos está mal. Alguien dejó el azúcar fuera.

films:night-shift-observatory.speaker: Narrator
films:night-shift-observatory.line: Nobody answers. The radio on the desk is tuned to a frequency that stopped transmitting in nineteen ninety-eight, and she keeps it on because the static is easier to work with than silence.
films:night-shift-observatory.translation: Nadie contesta. La radio del escritorio está sintonizada a una frecuencia que dejó de transmitir en mil novecientos noventa y ocho, y ella la deja encendida porque la estática es más fácil de trabajar que el silencio.

films:night-shift-observatory.speaker: Narrator
films:night-shift-observatory.line: The static does not answer either. But she asks again, and then again, because the question is not really for the radio.
films:night-shift-observatory.translation: La estática tampoco contesta. Pero pregunta otra vez, y luego otra, porque la pregunta no es realmente para la radio.

films:night-shift-observatory.speaker: Dr. Reyes
films:night-shift-observatory.line: The plate is finished. One hundred and two exposures. It is the clearest night of the year so far, and there is nobody here to see it with.
films:night-shift-observatory.translation: La placa está terminada. Ciento dos exposiciones. Es la noche más clara del año hasta ahora, y no hay nadie aquí para verlo con ella.

films:night-shift-observatory.speaker: Narrator
films:night-shift-observatory.line: She closes the dome at sunrise. It takes forty minutes and she does it alone, as she has done for six years.
films:night-shift-observatory.translation: Cierra la cúpula al amanecer. Tarda cuarenta minutos y lo hace sola, como lleva haciendo seis años.

films:night-shift-observatory.speaker: Narrator
films:night-shift-observatory.line: The static keeps its shape. It is the only company that has never needed her to explain why she is still awake.
films:night-shift-observatory.translation: La estática mantiene su forma. Es la única compañía que nunca ha necesitado que le explique por qué sigue despierta.
